source_text: 1. De fine vero et consummatione omnium iam quidem et in superioribus pro viribus nostris disseruimus, secundum quod divinae seripturae indulsit auctoritas, quae sufficere ad instructionem putamus, paucis etiam nune ammonitis, quoniam in hune nos locum quaestionis ordo perduxit. Igitur summum bonum, ad quod natura rationabilis universa festinat, qui etiam finis omnium dicitur, a quam plurimis etiam philosophorum hoe modo terminatur, quia summum bonum sit, prout possibile est, similem fieri deo. Sed hoc non tam ipsorum inventum, quam ex divinis libris ab eis adsumptum puto. Hoc namque indieat Moyses ante omnes, cum primam conditionem hominis enarrat dicens: “Et dixit deus: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram”. Tum deinde addit: “Et fecit deus hominem, ad imaginem dei fecit illum, masculum et feminam fecit eos, et benedixit eos”. Hoe ergo quod dixit “ad imaginem del fecit eum” et de similitudine siluit, non aliud indicat nisi quod -imaginis- quidem dignitatem in prima conditione percepit, "similitudinis vero ei perfectio in consummatione servata est: scilicet ut ipse sibi eam propriae industriae studiis ex dei imitatione conscisceret, quo possibilitate sibi perfectionis in initiis data per ‘imaginis’ dignitatem, in fine demum per operum expletionem perfectam sibi ipse ‘similitudinem’ consummaret. Sed apertius haec et evidentius ita se habere lohannes apostolus definit, hoc modo pronuntians: “Filioli, nondum. scimus quid futuri sumus; si vero revelatus nobis fuerit” (de salvatore sine dubio dicens) “similes ilh erimus”. Per quod certissime indicat et finem omnium, quem adhuc sibi dicit ignotum, et similitudinem dei sperandam, quae pro meritorum perfectione praestabitur. Ipse quoque dominus in evangelio haec eadem non solum futura, verum etiam sui intercessione futura designat, dum ipse hoe a patre discipulis suis impetrare dignatur dicens: “Pater, volo ut ubi ego sum et isti mecum sint”; et “sicut ego et tu unum sumus, ita et isti in nobis unum sint”. In quo iam videtur ipsa similitudo, si dici potest, proficere et ex simili “unum- lam fieri, pro eo sine dubio quod in consummatione vel fine "omnia et in omnibus deus- est. In quo requiritur a nonnullis, si ratio naturae corporeae, quamvis expurgatae ad liquidum et penitus spiritalis effectae, non videatur obsistere vel ad similitudinis dignitatem vel ad unitatis proprietatem, quod naturae divinae, quae utique principaliter incorporea est, nec similis videatur posse dici quae in corpore est natura nec unum cum ea vere ac merito designari, maxime cum id, quod ‘unum est filius cum patres, ad naturae proprietatem referendum fidei veritas doceat. 2. Cum ergo in fine “deus esse omnia et in omnibus- promittatur, sieut consequens est, non est opinandum venire ad illum finem animalia vel pecora vel bestias, ne etiam in animalibus aut pecoribus vel bestiis deus inesse designetur; sed nec ligna vel lapides, ne in his quoque esse dicatur deus. lta ne ullam quidem malitiam ad illum finem putandum est pervenire, ne dum ‘in omnibus deus esse- dicitur, etiam in aliquo malitiae vasculo inesse dicatur. Nam etiamsi nunc quoque ubique et ‘in omnibus esse- dicimus deum, pro eo quod nihil potest esse vacuum deo, non tamen ita esse dicimus, ut “omnia- sit nune in quibus est. Unde diligentius intuendum est quale est hoc, quod perfeetionem beatitudinis rerumque finem significat, quod non solum ‘in omnibus esse- dicitur deus, sed etiam -ommia- esse dicitur deus. Quae sint ergo ista ‘omnia”, quae deus futurus sit ‘in omnibuse, requiramus. 3. Et ego quidem arbitror quia hoc, quod ‘in omnibus omnia essedicitur deus, significet etiam in singulis eum ‘omnia esse. Per singulos autem “omnia- erit hoc modo, ut quidquid rationabilis mens, expurgata omni vitiorum faece atque omni penitus abstersa nube malitiae, vel sentire vel intellegere vel cogitare potest, -omnia- deus sit nec ultra iam aliquid aliud nisi deum sentiat, deum cogitet, deum videat, deum teneat, omnis motus sui deus modus et mensura sit; et ita erit ei ‘omnia’ deus: non enim 1am ultra mali bonique discretio, quia nusquam malum (-omnia’ enim ei deus est, cui iam non adiacet malum), nec (aun ultra ex arbore sciendi ‘bonum et malum- edere concupiscet qui sem- ^ per in bono est, et cui ‘omnia” deus est. Si ergo finis ad principium reparatus et rerum exitus conlatus initüs restituet illum statum, quem tune habuit natura rationabilis, cum de ligno sciendi -bonum et malumedere non egebat, ut amoto omni malitiae sensu et ad sincerum purumque deterso solus qui est unus deus bonus hie ei fiat ‘omnia-, et non in paucis aliquibus vel pluribus sed ut ‘in omnibus- ipse sit ‘omnia”, cum iam nusquam “morse nusquam -aculeus- mortis, nusquam omnino malum: tunc vere deus ‘omnia in omnibus- erit. Verum istam perfectionem ae beatitudinem rationabilium naturarum ita demum quidam permanere in eo statu quo supra diximus putant, id est ut deum -0mnla- habeant, et deus eis sit ‘omnia’, si nullatenus eas societas naturae corporalis amoveat. Alioquin aestimant gloriam summae beatitudinis inpediri, si materialis substantiae interseratur admixtio. De qua re plenius nobis in superioribus quae oecarrere potuerunt pertractata atque digesta sunt. 4. Nune vero quoniam apud apostolum Paulum mentionem ‘spiritalis corporis invenimus, qualiter etiam inde sentiri debeat de hoc, tantummodo prout possumus requiramus. Quantum ergo sensus noster capere potest, qualitatem spiritalis corporis talem quandam esse sentimus, in quo inhabitare deceat non solum sanctas quasque perfectasque animas, verum etiam omnem illam ereaturam, quae ‘liberabitur a servitute corruptionis. De quo corpore etiam illud apostolus dixit quia “domum habemus non manu factam, aeternam in caelis”, id est in mansionibus beatorum. Ex hoc ergo coniecturam capere possumus, quantae puritatis, quantae subtilitatis quantaeque gloriae sit qualitas corporis ilhus, si eonparationem faciamus eius ad ea, quae nune, licet caelestia sint et splendidissima corpora, ‘manu facta- tamen sunt et visibilia. De illo autem dicitur domus esse ‘non manu facta’, sed “aeberna in caelis. Quia ergo “quae videntur temporalia sunt, quae autem non videntur aeterna sunt”, omnibus his corporibus, quae sive in terris sive in caelis videmus et quae videri possunt et -manu factasunt et “aeterna- non sunt, multa longe praelatione praecelht illud, quod et visibile non est nec -manu- factum est, sed ‘aeternum” est. Ex qua conparatione conici potest, quantus decor, quantus splendor quantusque fulgor sit ‘corporis spiritaliss et verum esse illud, quod dictum est, quia “oculus non vidit nec auris audivit nec in cor hominis ascendit quae praeparavit deus his, qui diligunt eum”. Non autem dubitandum est naturam corporis huius nostri voluntate dei, qui talem fecit eam, usque ad illam qualitatem subtilissimi et purissimi ae splendidissimi Sc corporis posse a creatore perduci, prout rerum status vocaverit et meritum rationabilis naturae poposcerit. Denique cum varietate et diversitate mundus indiguit, per diversas rerum facies speciesque omni famulatu praebuit se materia conditori, utpote domino et creatori suo, quo diversas caelestium terrenorumque ex ea duceret formas. Cum vero res ad illud coeperint festinare, “ut sint omnes unum”, sicut est ‘pater cum filo unum” consequenter intellegi datur quod, ubi omnes -unumsunt, iam diversitas non erit. 5. Propterea namque etiam ‘novissimus inimicus’, qui “mors- appellatur, destrui dicitur, ut neque ultra triste sit aliquid, ubi mors non est, neque diversum sit, ubi non est inimicus. -Destrui- sane -novissimus inimicus- ita intellegendus est, non ut substantia eius quae a deo faeta est pereat, sed ut propositum et voluntas inimica, quae non a deo sed ( ab ipso processit, intereat. ‘Destruetur’ ergo, non ut non sit, sed ut “inimicus’ et “mors’ non sit. -Nihil- enim omnipotenti ‘inpossibile est”, nee insanabile est aliquid factori suo; propterea enim fecit omnia, ut essent; et ea, quae facta sunt, ut essent, non esse non possunt. Propter quod immutationem quidem varietatemque recipient, ita ut pro meritis vel in meliore vel in deteriore habeantur statu; substantialem vero interitum ea, quae a deo ad hoc facta sunt, ut essent et permanerent, recipere non possunt. Non enim ea, quae opinione vulgi interire ereduntur, eontinuo etiam vel fidei vel veritatis ratio ea interisse consentit. Denique caro nostra ab inperitis et infidelibus ita post mortem deperire aestimatur, ut nihil prorsus substantiae suae reliquum habere eredatur. Nos vero, qui resurrectionem eius credimus, immutationem eius tantummodo per mortem factam intellegimus, substantiam vero certum est permanere et voluntate creatoris sui certo quo tempore reparari rursus ad vitam, atque iterum permutationem eius fieri; ut quae primo fuit earo “ex terra terrena”, tum deinde dissoluta per mortem et iterum facta “cinis ae terra” (“quoniam terra es” inquit “et in terram 1015.) rursum resuscitetur e terra et post hoc iam, prout meritum inhabitantis animae poposcerit, in gloriam ‘corporis’ proficiat ‘spiritalis”. 6. In hune ergo statum omnem hane nostram substantiam corporalem putandum est perducendam, tune cum omnia restituentur, ut -unum” sint, et eum deus fuerit -omnia in omnibus. Quod tamen non ad subitum fieri sed paulatim et per partes intellegendum est, infinitis et immensis labentibus saeculis, cum sensim et per singulos emendatio fuerit et correctio prosecuta, praecurrentibus alüs et velociore cursu ad summa tendentibus, alüs vero proximo quoque spatio insequentibus, tum deinde aliis longe posterius: et sic per multos et innumeros ordines proficientium et deo se ex inimicis reconcilantium pervenitur usque ad “novissimum inimieume, qui dicitur ‘mors’, ut etiam ipse -destruatur., ne ultra sit inimicus. Cum ergo restitutae fuerint omnes rationabiles animae in huiuscemodi statum, tune etiam natura huius corporis nostri im ‘spiritalis corporis’ gloriam perducetur. Sieut-enim de rationabilibus naturis videmus non alias esse, quae pro peccatis in indignitate vixerint, et alias, quae pro meritis ad beatitudinem invitatae sint, sed has easdem, quae antea fuerant peccatrices, conversas postmodum et deo reconciliatas videmus ad beatitudinem revocari: ita etiam de natura corporis sentiendum est quod non aliud corpus est, quo nune in ignobilitate et in corruptione et in infirmitate utimur, et aliud erit illud, quo in incorruptione et in virtute et in gloria utemur, sed hoc idem abiectis his infirmitatibus, in quibus nune est, in gloriam transmutabitur, -spiritaleeffectum, ut quod fuit ‘indignitatis vas’, hoc ipsum expurgatum fiat -vas honoris- et beatitudinis habitaculum. In quo statu etiam permanere semper et immutabiliter creatoris voluntate eredendum est, fidem rei faciente sententia apostoli Pauli dicentis: “Domum habemus non manu factam, aeternam in caelis”. Non enim seeundum quosdam Graecorum philosophos praeter hoc corpus, quod ex quattuor constat elementis, aliud quintum corpus, quod per omnia aliud sit et diversum ab hoc nostro eorpore, fides ecclesiae recipit; quoniam neque ex scripturis sanetis vel suspicionem aliquam de his proferre quis potest neque ipsa rerum consequentia hoe recipi patitur, maxime cum manifeste definiat sanctus apostolus quia non nova aliqua. corpora resurgentibus a mortuis dentur, sed haec ipsa, quae viventes habuerant, ex deterioribus in melius transformata recipiant. Ait enim: “Seminatur corpus animale, resurget, corpus spiritale” et “seminatur in corjruptione, resurget in incorruptione; seminatur in infirmitate, resurget in virtute; seminatur in ignobilitate, resurget in gloria”. Sicut ergo profeetus est homini quidam, ut cum sit prius animalis homo- nec intellegat ‘quae sunt spiritus dei, veniat in hoe per eruditionem, ut efficiatur ‘spiritalis’ et -diiudicet omnia, ipse vero a nemine diindicetur’: ita etiam de corporis statu putandum est quod idem ipsum corpus, quod nune pro ministerio animae nuncupatum est animale, per profectum quendam, cum anima adiuncta deo ‘unus’ cum eo “spiritus” fuerit effecta, iam tum corpus quasi spiritui ministrans in statum qualitatemque proficiat spiritalem, maxime cum, sicut saepe ostendimus, talis a conditore facta sit natura corporea, ut in quamcumque voluerit vel res poposcerit qualitatem facile subsequatur. 7. Omnis igitur haec ratio hoe continet, quod duas generales naturas eondidert deus: naturam visibilem, id est corpoream, et naturam invisibilem, quae est incorporea. Istae vero duae naturae diversas sui recipiunt permutationes. llla quidem invisibilis, quae et rationabilis est, animo propositoque mutatur pro eo quod arbitrii sui libertate donata est; et per hoe aliquando in bonis, aliquando in contrariis invenitur. Haec vero natura corporea substantialem recipit permutationem; unde et ad omne quodcumque moliri vel fabricari vel retractare voluerit artifex omnium deus, materiae huius habet in omnibus famulatum, ut in quaseumque vult formas vel species, prout rerum merita deposeunt, naturam corpoream transmutet et transferat. Quod evidenter propheta designans ait: “Deus” inquit “qui facit omnia et transmutat”., S. Iam sane illud quaerendum est, si tunc, cum erit “deus omnia in omnibus, in consummatione omnium universa corporis natura una specie constabit, et omnis qualitas corporis illa sola erit, quae in illa inenarrabili gloria fulgebit, quae spiritalis eorporis futura esse sentienda est. Si enim recte accipimus id, quod in initio libri sui Moyses scribit dicens: “In principio fecit deus caelum et terram”, hoc esse “principium- totius creaturae, ad hoc -principium- finem omnium consummationemque convenit revocarl, id est ut illud caelum atque illa terra habitatio et requies sit piorum; ita ut prius “terrae- illius saneti quique et ‘mansueti hereditatem capiant-, quoniam quidem hoe et lex et prophetae et evangelium docet. In qua terra puto esse veras illas et vivas formas illius observantiae, quam Moyses per -legis umbram- tradebat. De quibus dictum est quia “exemplario et umbrae deserviunt caelestium, hi seilicet, qui serviebant in lege. Sed et ad ipsum Moysen dietum est: “Vide ut faeias omnia secundum formam et similitudinem, quae tibi ostensa est in monte”. Unde mihi videtur quod, sicut in hae terra ‘lex paedagogus- quidam fuit eorum, qui ‘ad Christum- ab ipsa perduci deberent, eruditi ab ea et instituti, ut facilius possent post institutionem legis perfectiora quaeque Christi instituta suscipere, ita etiam illa terra, sanetos quosque suscipiens, verae et aeternae legis institutionibus eos prius imbuat et informet, quo facilius etiam caeli perfecta illa et quibus addi iam nihil potest instituta patiantur; in quo vere erit illud, quod -aeternum- dieitur ‘evangeliuni’ et ‘“testamentum’ semper “novum”, quod numquam ‘veterescet”. 9. Hoe itaque modo in consummatione ac restitutione omnium fieri putandum est, ut paulatim proficientes et ascendentes modo et ordine perveniant primo ad terram illam et eruditionem, quae in ea est, in qua ad meliora et illa, quibus iam addi nihil potest, instituta praeparentur. Post ‘actores: enim et “proeuratores- Christus dominus, qui est rex omnium, regnum ipse suscipiet, id est post eruditionem sanetarum virtutum eos, qui eum capere possunt secundum quod sapientia est, ipse instruet, regnans in eis tamdiu usquequo eos etiam patri subieiat qui sibi subdidit omnia” id est ut, cum capaces del fuerint effecti, sit eis deus omnia in omnibus. Tune ergo consequenter etiam natura corporea illum summum et cui addi iam nihil possit recipiet statum. Hactenus nobis etiam corporeae naturae vel spiritalis corporis ratione diseussa, arbitrio legentis relinquimus ex utroque quod melius iudieaverit eligendum. ^ Nos vero in his finem libri tertii faciamus.
pass_a_gloss: We have indeed already discussed the end and consummation of all things in the preceding sections according to the authority of divine scripture as much as our abilities allow, which we think is sufficient for instruction, and we are also warning a few now, because the order of the question has led us to this place. Therefore, the highest good, to which the entire rational nature hastens, which is also called the end of all things, is defined by very many philosophers in this way, because the highest good is to become as similar to God as possible. But this is not their invention, rather it is taken from divine books. For Moses indicates this first of all when he narrates the first condition of man, saying: And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness. Then he adds: And God made man, he made him in the image of God, he made them male and female, and he blessed them. Therefore, when he said he made him in the image of God and was silent about the likeness, it indicates nothing other than that he perceived the dignity of the image in the first condition, but the perfection of the likeness is reserved for the consummation, so that he himself might acquire it by his own industry and studies, imitating God, whereby the possibility of perfection given to him in the beginning through the dignity of the image, he might finally consummate the likeness to himself through the fulfillment of works. But the apostle John defines this more clearly and evidently, saying: My little children, we do not yet know what we will be; if indeed he who is our Savior has been revealed to us, we will be like him. By which he certainly indicates both the end of all things, which he says is still unknown to him, and the likeness of God which is to be hoped for, and which will be granted according to the perfection of merits. The Lord himself also indicates this in the gospel, not only that it will happen, but also that it will happen through his intercession, when he deigns to ask the Father for his disciples, saying: Father, I want them to be where I am, and that they may be one with us, just as you and I are one. In which it seems that the likeness itself is already progressing, and from being similar, they will become one, undoubtedly because in the consummation or end, God will be all in all. This requires that the nature of the corporeal, even if purified and made completely spiritual, does not seem to hinder either the dignity of likeness or the property of unity, which is the nature of the divine, which is certainly incorporeal, and it does not seem possible to say that what is in the body is similar to it, nor can it be truly and deservedly called one with it, especially since the truth of faith teaches that what is one with the Father and the Son is to be referred to the property of nature. When therefore it is promised that in the end God will be all in all, it is not to be thought that animals or cattle or beasts will come to this end, nor even that God will be in them; nor will trees or stones, so that God may not be said to be in them. So also, no evil is to be thought to reach this end, lest when it is said that God is in all things, it may also be said that he is in some vessel of evil. For even if we say that God is now everywhere and in all things, because nothing can be empty of God, we do not say that all things are now in him. Hence it is to be considered more carefully what this is, which signifies the perfection of beatitude and the end of things, that God is not only said to be in all things, but also that all things are said to be God. What then are these all things, which God will be in all things, we must ask. And I indeed think that when it is said that God is all in all, it also signifies that he is all in each individual. But in each individual, all things will be this way, so that whatever the rational mind, purified of all filth of vices and completely cleansed of every cloud of malice, can sense or understand or think, God will be all things, and it will no longer sense or think or see anything else except God; and God will be the measure and norm of all its movements; and so God will be all things to it: for there will no longer be a distinction between good and evil, because evil will nowhere exist, since God will be all things to the one to whom no evil adheres, and who no longer desires to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because it is always in the good, and to whom God is all things. If therefore the end is restored to the beginning, and the exit of things is compared to the initiations, it will restore that state which rational nature had when it did not need to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, so that with all sense of malice removed, and the one who is the only good God being purified and cleansed, he may become all things to it, and not in a few or many things, but so that he himself may be all things in all things, when there is nowhere death, nowhere a sting of death, nowhere any evil at all: then indeed God will be all in all. But this perfection and beatitude of rational natures is thought by some to remain in that state which we mentioned above, that is, so that they may have God as all things, and God may be all things to them, if the society of corporeal nature does not remove them from it. Otherwise, they think that the glory of the highest beatitude is hindered, if the mixture of material substance intervenes. About which thing we have discussed more fully in the preceding sections what could have occurred and been digested. Now, since we find a mention of the spiritual body with the apostle Paul, we must ask how it is to be understood from this, as much as we can. As far as our sense can grasp, we think that the quality of the spiritual body is of such a kind that it is fitting for not only holy and perfect souls to inhabit it, but also for all that creation which will be liberated from the servitude of corruption. About which body the apostle also said that we have a house not made by hand, eternal in the heavens, that is, in the dwellings of the blessed. From this, we can take a conjecture about the quality of that body, how great is its purity, subtlety, and glory, if we make a comparison with those things which are now, although they are celestial and most splendid bodies, yet they are made by hand and visible. But about that body, it is said to be a house not made by hand, but eternal in the heavens. Because what is seen is temporal, but what is not seen is eternal, all these bodies which we see in the earth or in the heavens, and which can be seen, and are made by hand, and are not eternal, are far surpassed by that which is not visible, nor made by hand, but is eternal. From this comparison, it can be conjectured how great is the beauty, splendor, and radiance of the spiritual body, and that it is true what has been said, that the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him. There is no doubt that the nature of this our body, by the will of God who made it, can be led to that quality of the most subtle, pure, and splendid spiritual body, as the state of things and the merit of rational nature may require. Finally, when the world was in need of variety and diversity, it provided itself as material for the creator, as its lord and master, to draw from it various forms of celestial and terrestrial things. But when things begin to hasten to that end, that all may be one, as the Father is one with the Son, it is consequently understood that where all are one, there will no longer be diversity. Therefore, the last enemy, who is called death, is said to be destroyed, so that there may no longer be anything sad, where death is not, nor anything diverse, where there is no enemy. The last enemy is to be destroyed, not so that the substance which God made may perish, but so that the hostile proposal and will, which did not come from God but from itself, may come to an end. It will be destroyed, not so that it may not exist, but so that it may not be an enemy and death. For nothing is impossible for the omnipotent, nor is anything incurable for its maker; for this reason, he made all things so that they might exist; and what has been made, so that it might exist, cannot not exist. On account of which, they receive a change and diversity, so that according to merits they may be in a better or worse state; but the substantial destruction, those things which God made so that they might exist and remain, cannot receive. For not everything which the common opinion thinks perishes, does the reason of faith or truth consent to its perishing. Finally, our flesh is thought by the unskilled and the faithless to perish after death, so that it is believed to have no remainder of its substance. But we, who believe in its resurrection, understand its change, but not its substantial destruction, and we are certain that it will remain and will be restored to life again by the will of its creator at a certain time, and its transformation will happen again; so that what was first earthy flesh, then dissolved through death, and again made into ashes and earth, may rise again from the earth, and after this, according to the merit of the inhabiting soul, may advance to the glory of the spiritual body. Therefore, we think that our entire corporeal substance will be led to this state, when all things will be restored, so that they may be one, and God will be all in all. But this is not to be understood as happening suddenly, but gradually and in parts, over infinite and immense ages, as the correction and emendation of things will have been pursued, with some preceding and running more quickly to the highest things, and others following at a closer or more distant interval: and so, through many and innumerable orders of those who are advancing and reconciling themselves to God, we come to the last enemy, who is called death, so that it also may be destroyed, and no longer be an enemy. When therefore all rational souls have been restored to this state, then also the nature of this our body will be led to the glory of the spiritual body. Just as we see that those who lived in indignity on account of sins, and those who were invited to beatitude on account of merits, are not different, but the same, who were previously sinners, and afterwards converted and reconciled to God, and called to beatitude: so also, it is to be thought that the nature of the body is not one thing, which we now use in indignity and corruption and infirmity, and another thing, which we will use in incorruption and virtue and glory, but this same body, having cast off these infirmities, will be transformed into glory, made spiritual, so that what was a vessel of indignity may become a vessel of honor and a dwelling place of beatitude. In which state, it is also to be believed that it will remain forever and immutably by the will of the creator, the sentence of the apostle Paul making faith, saying: We have a house not made by hand, eternal in the heavens. For the faith of the church does not receive, as some of the Greek philosophers do, another body, a fifth body, which is different from this our body, and diverse from it; since neither the holy scriptures nor the consequence of things allows this to be received, especially since the holy apostle defines that the resurrected will not receive new bodies, but these same bodies which they had while living, transformed from worse to better. For he says: It is sown a natural body, it will rise a spiritual body; it is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in infirmity, it will rise in virtue; it is sown in ignobility, it will rise in glory. Just as a man is said to be animal, and does not understand what things are of the spirit of God, and comes to this through education, so that he may become spiritual and judge all things, and no one may judge him: so also, it is to be thought that the body, which is now called animal, because it is ministering to the soul, will advance to a spiritual state, when the soul, joined to God, will have become one spirit with him. And when the prophet says: God who makes all things and transforms them, it is evident that he indicates the transformation of all things. Now, it is to be asked, if when God will be all in all, in the consummation of all things, the entire nature of the body will consist of one species, and all quality of the body will be that which will shine in that inexpressible glory, which the spiritual body is to be. If we rightly understand what Moses writes at the beginning of his book, saying: In the beginning, God made the heaven and the earth, this is the beginning of all creation, to which the end and consummation of all things is to be referred, that is, so that that heaven and that earth may be the dwelling and rest of the pious; so that first the meek and the gentle may inherit the earth, as the law and the prophets and the gospel teach. In which earth, I think, are the true and living forms of that observance, which Moses handed down through the shadow of the law. About which it is said that they serve as a copy and shadow of the celestial things, those who served in the law. And it was said to Moses himself: See that you make all things according to the form and likeness which was shown to you on the mountain. From which it seems to me that, just as the law was a kind of pedagogue for those who were to be led to Christ, and they were instructed and educated by it, so that they might more easily receive the perfect institutions of Christ after the instruction of the law: so also, that earth, receiving the saints, will first imbue and inform them with the institutions of the true and eternal law, so that they may more easily bear the perfect institutions of the heavens, which cannot be added to; in which truly will be that which is called the eternal gospel and the new testament, which will never grow old. This, therefore, is to be thought to happen in the consummation and restitution of all things, that those who are advancing and ascending may come first to that earth and its education, in which they are prepared for better things, and those things to which nothing can be added. For after the pedagogues and precursors, Christ the Lord, who is the king of all, will receive the kingdom, that is, after the education of holy virtues, he will instruct those who can receive him, according to wisdom, reigning in them, until he subjects them to the Father, who has subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all to them. Then, consequently, the nature of the body will also receive that highest and most perfect state. We have discussed the reason of the corporeal and spiritual body as far as we could, and we leave it to the judgment of the reader to choose what is better from both. We, however, will make an end to this book.

pass_b_english: We have already discussed the end and consummation of all things in the preceding sections, according to the authority of divine scripture, as much as our abilities allow, which we think is sufficient for instruction. The highest good, to which the entire rational nature hastens, is also called the end of all things, and is defined by many philosophers as becoming as similar to God as possible. But this is not their invention, rather it is taken from divine books, such as when Moses says, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' (Genesis 1:26-27). The apostle John also defines this, saying, 'My little children, we do not yet know what we will be; if indeed he who is our Savior has been revealed to us, we will be like him.' The Lord himself indicates this in the gospel, saying, 'Father, I want them to be where I am, and that they may be one with us, just as you and I are one.' This requires that the nature of the corporeal, even if purified and made completely spiritual, does not seem to hinder either the dignity of likeness or the property of unity, which is the nature of the divine. When it is promised that in the end God will be all in all, it is not to be thought that animals or cattle or beasts will come to this end, nor even that God will be in them; nor will trees or stones, so that God may not be said to be in them. The last enemy, who is called death, is said to be destroyed, so that there may no longer be anything sad, where death is not, nor anything diverse, where there is no enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26). The nature of this our body, by the will of God who made it, can be led to that quality of the most subtle, pure, and splendid spiritual body, as the state of things and the merit of rational nature may require. Finally, our flesh is thought by the unskilled and the faithless to perish after death, so that it is believed to have no remainder of its substance. But we, who believe in its resurrection, understand its change, but not its substantial destruction, and we are certain that it will remain and will be restored to life again by the will of its creator at a certain time, and its transformation will happen again; so that what was first earthy flesh, then dissolved through death, and again made into ashes and earth, may rise again from the earth, and after this, according to the merit of the inhabiting soul, may advance to the glory of the spiritual body, which is sown a natural body and will rise a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44). Therefore, we think that our entire corporeal substance will be led to this state, when all things will be restored, so that they may be one, and God will be all in all.
